source.title: Critical Data Size of Language Models from a Grokking Perspective
source.authors: Xuekai Zhu; Yao Fu; Bo-Wen Zhou; Zhou-Han Lin

page_placements.theme: Delayed generalization, grokking and critical learning transitions

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present. Some figure content and formatting are flattened, but the relevant text is readable.
record.tranche_reason: The paper experimentally varies data size, training time, and model size and reports test-accuracy outcomes relevant to the proposed curves, using a grokking configuration rather than the original double-descent method.
record.gate_note: Rows cover the paper's own test-accuracy results from sample-wise and model-wise grokking experiments. Related-work descriptions of other papers are not rows. Training-accuracy and parameter-norm observations are omitted because they do not themselves measure the claim's test-error curves.
record.test_reason: The paper studies grokking and a critical data size, citing deep double descent only as background and as loose framing for its hypothesis. None of its results measures a double-descent shape. All models memorize the training set, so no curve is placed against an interpolation threshold. The test-accuracy-over-steps curves are induced grokking trajectories (flat, then rising), not test-error fall-rise-fall. Sample-wise sweeps show data helping, without a near-threshold probe. The model-wise result averages accuracy over data fractions. These results do not bear on whether V1–V7 hold, so no verdicts are given.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude there is a critical data size marking a shift from quick memorization to slow generalization. They frame it as a Data Efficiency Hypothesis with insufficiency, sufficiency and surplus regimes. They find the critical size grows with model size, and all results hold under a simplistic, specially induced grokking configuration.
record.recipe_differences: The paper uses uniform data pruning and a grokking configuration with rescaled initialization and weight decay on language-model tasks; it does not reproduce the original double-descent procedure.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcomes vary with dataset size, model hidden size and layer count, and the grokking configuration; the text also notes that initialization rescaling and weight decay affect convergence.

fits_no_version.finding: Under the induced grokking configuration, test accuracy jumps long after training accuracy reaches 100%. Examples: IMDB about 50% to 87% after about 350k steps; modular addition reaches 100% at about 3500 steps.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Delayed generalization (grokking) under large initialization and small weight decay

fits_no_version.finding: A critical data size exists below which models memorize but do not generalize, and above which generalization speeds up. Examples: modular addition with 1000–1500 samples stays under 50% test accuracy; on Yelp, more data speeds convergence.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Critical data size for generalization under grokking

fits_no_version.finding: On IMDB, accuracy averaged over data fractions falls as hidden size grows from 16 to 256. The critical data size grows with model size, which the authors liken to inverse scaling.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Larger models need more data to generalize under grokking; inverse scaling at low data

record.problems: The evidence comes from simplified models trained under a specially induced grokking configuration. Model-wise results are largely figure-based and include an average across data fractions rather than a fixed-data size curve. The authors note difficulty reproducing grokking on larger models and that training can be unstable on the instruction-tuning task.
record.rows_left_out: No otherwise qualifying results were left out.

untested.parts: No test-error curve over model size at fixed data relative to the interpolation threshold.
No epoch-wise test-error curve in a non-induced setting; grokking trajectories cannot show fall-rise-fall.
No sample sweep near an interpolation threshold.
Not tested; no label noise is used and regularization tuning is not tested for removing a peak.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's 'tests'/T2 classification and its V1–V3 verdicts should be dropped. The paper cites Nakkiran et al. only as background and as framing for its hypothesis. Its curves (step-wise accuracy, averages over data fractions) cannot show double-descent shapes. No label noise is used, and every model interpolates its training set. The setting is deliberately induced through rescaled initialization and weight decay.

versions.untested_parts: The paper varies hidden size and layer count on IMDB, but does not report a fall-rise-fall test-error curve aligned to the size that just fits the training set.
Training is discussed in steps rather than epochs; the paper studies grokking trajectories but does not report a fall-rise-fall test-error curve over time.
The paper varies sample size but does not isolate small increases in data specifically around an interpolation threshold while holding other conditions fixed.
No broad comparison across model classes testing general double descent.
No single effective-complexity measure is proposed or tested as predicting peak locations across axes.
The paper does not test label-noise dependence, triple or multiple descent, or disappearance of double descent under optimally tuned regularization.
The paper does not recount complexity using an effective number of parameters or test whether that turns second descent into a U-shaped curve.

rows.subject: 1-layer decoder-only Transformer
rows.operation_detail: Followed test accuracy during training under the grokking configuration.
rows.value: 100% test accuracy at approximately 3500 steps; the text describes delayed generalization after training accuracy reached 100% within the first 500 steps.
rows.note: The reported trajectory is delayed generalization, not the claimed fall-rise-fall test-error shape.
rows.check: Grokking trajectory produced by rescaled initialization and weight decay. Test accuracy over steps under an induced configuration, not epoch-wise double descent; there is no early test-error minimum followed by a rise. Marking it partial against V2 is unfounded.

rows.subject: 1-layer encoder-only Transformer (hidden-size sweep)
rows.size_stated: Hidden size 16 to 256, in increments of 16
rows.operation_detail: Varied hidden size and measured average test accuracy across data fractions.

conditions.value: mean accuracy across all data fractions

rows.value: Average accuracy decreases as hidden size increases; plotted values are figure only.
rows.note: The reported average trend does not show the claimed second descent; because it aggregates data fractions, it is not a controlled fixed-data size curve.
rows.check: Accuracy is averaged over data fractions 10–100%, so this is not a fixed-data size curve. Hidden sizes 16–256 all memorize the training set, so no interpolation threshold is crossed. This cannot show V1's peak or second descent.

rows.subject: Encoder-only Transformer (layer-count sweep)
rows.operation_detail: Varied layer count and data fraction and compared training curves.
rows.measure: Test accuracy / generalization across model depth and data sizes
rows.value: The text states that as layer count increases, larger data sizes are needed for effective generalization; curve values are figure only.
rows.note: No fall-rise-fall test-error curve by model size is reported.
rows.check: Layer sweep (2–6 layers) reported as training curves showing that more layers need more data. No test-error-vs-size curve around an interpolation threshold.

rows.subject: 1-layer decoder-only Transformer
rows.operation_detail: Varied the number of modular-addition training samples and measured test accuracy.
rows.measure: Test accuracy across training sample sizes
rows.value: With 1000 and 1500 training samples, test accuracy cannot reach 50%; at the critical size the model reaches 100% test accuracy after approximately 3500 steps. The data-size curve is figure only.
rows.note: The reported sample-wise trend is improved generalization with sufficient added data, not increased test error near the critical size.
rows.check: The sample-size sweep shows generalization appearing above a critical data size. It does not probe test error near an interpolation threshold, since all sizes memorize. Marking it reversed against V3 overreaches.

rows.subject: 1-layer encoder-only Transformer
rows.operation_detail: Varied the IMDB training-data fraction and measured test accuracy and generalization steps.

conditions.value: varied; individual fractions not specified in the text

rows.value: Before the critical threshold, generalization is approximately 67%; as the data fraction grows, it gradually reaches approximately 80%.
rows.note: The described test-accuracy result improves with more data; the text also says generalization steps stabilize around 400,000 after the critical size.
rows.check: IMDB data-fraction sweep with accuracy rising from ~67% to ~80%. No interpolation-threshold probe, so it cannot show V3. The ~67%/~80% values come from a step-wise analysis figure.

rows.subject: 1-layer encoder-only Transformer
rows.operation_detail: Varied the Yelp training-data fraction and measured test performance.
rows.value: Reducing the data size from 100% to 10% results in about a 5% decrease in performance; additional data did not lead to an improvement, but accelerated convergence.
rows.note: The text reports no rise in test error from adding data; additional data is described as accelerating convergence.
rows.check: Yelp: more data speeds convergence without changing performance. Not a V3 test; no near-threshold design.

relation.reason: Double descent supplies background and loose theoretical framing; the reported results concern delayed generalization rather than double-descent curves.

tranche.reason: The experiments study induced grokking and critical data size; they neither test a double-descent claim version nor use double descent as an experimental tool.
